SOVIET EARTH SATELLITE
speechtext:
North):
1.	Has the earth satellite been fired in accordance with any agreement arrived at during the international geophysical year?
2.	Is the Soviet earth satellite infringing on the air space above Canada?
3.	How far vertically does the sovereignty of Canada extend?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SOVIET EARTH SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the first part of that question is that there was no formal agreement in connection with the international geophysical year pertaining to the launching of an earth satellite, and in any event the U.S.S.R. has stated that it did not launch the satellite in pursuance of any arrangement in that regard.
With respect to parts 2 and 3 of this question I might answer them together. Under the present generally accepted rules of international law the space above the territory of each nation extends to the upper limits of the atmosphere. Although the Soviet union did not join in the international civil aviation organization convention of 1944 it was decided that every state has complete and universal sovereignty over air space above its territory.
Until recently air space for the purpose of state sovereignty and control had been thought to vary between the heights of 60 and 80 miles. There has been some discussion in regard to this matter recently by those versed in international law. Professor John Cooper of the school of international air law at McGill University recently reported favouring a limit of 300 miles for the air space; however, there has been no determination in this regard. Recent events in science do suggest an early review of the present principles of international law applicable to the question of sovereignty over the air space.

subsubtopic: CLOSING DOWN OF HOWE SOUND COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my absence from the house yesterday a number of questions were asked concerning the reported closing down of operations by the Howe Sound Company at Britannia Beach. In so far as these questions were directed specifically to myself I think they can be answered in one statement, as follows. Both questions, Mr. Speaker, dealt with matters of government policy in so far as they concern support or protection for the base metals industry. The present situation of the mine derives from the present condition of the market in base metals, which in turn derives from a number of factors, many of them international in nature and outside the control of this government.
I may say that the whole situation is being actively examined in line with representations received, and when a decision has been reached it will be communicated to this house in the usual way. Meanwhile the mine is still operating, and should the officials in charge of its operations decide that it is no longer economical to continue in production on account of the low world prices presently prevailing in zinc and copper, then the full resources of the Department of Labour will be at the disposal of the workers involved.

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Right	Hon.	J.	G.	Diefenbaker	(Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre and also, I think, by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in connection with the results of investigations on the part of the board of transport commissioners into Trans-Canada Pipe Lines explosions in the province of Manitoba, and also one at Mortlach in the province of Saskatchewan.
The board of transport commissioners reports that an investigation has taken place not only in these cases but also in all cases where there have been explosions on pipe lines under the board of transport commission's jurisdiction. They have not been able to determine exactly the reason for the explosions. They find that the breaks which have occurred appear to have been in the longitudinal seam welds, but the reason for the breaks has not been determined. Testing was carried out under a pressure of 110 per cent of the maximum allowable working pressure. In addition, the piping is inspected visually at the factory and on the job. What has happened must have been the result of latent and as yet undiscoverable defects. The company has also instituted an investigation and is doing everything it can to ascertain the reason for the explosions, but as yet no determination of the cause has been arrived at.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, November 5, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Brooks-Mr. Cassel-man in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the War Veterans' Allowance Act, 1952, to increase the monthly rates of certain allowances and permissible income; to extend the provisions of the act to additional classes of veterans, widows and orphans; and to increase the salaries of the members of the war veterans allowance board.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES, INCOME, COVERAGE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have always had a very high regard for the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I have been associated with him on veterans committees for the past 22 years, and during that time I have come to know him as a persistent fighter in the interests of the veterans. We in the Social Credit group and the C.C.F. group along with other members of his party have always joined with him in trying to improve the conditions of the veterans. But of course it will continue to be our duty in this group and in the C.C.F. to continue that fight if for no other reason than that of strengthening his hand. He himself, of course, will no longer need to fight for these things in the house, but he will have to fight with the cabinet and the treasury board in order to obtain the funds to reach the objective that he himself has striven for in the past.

I think the minister is to be commended for this measure. It is in line with the proposals that have been made by him in the past, and I trust that this measure will be referred to a special committee on veterans affairs or, better still, that he will carry out one of the things he has advocated in the past, namely the setting up of a standing committee on veterans affairs and then refer this measure to that standing committee.
I have always felt that the War Veterans' Allowance Act was one of the most important acts coming under the Department of Veterans Affairs. I say that because the War Veterans' Allowance Act may be regarded as the veteran's last resort in case of need. For example a disabled veteran, unable to get a pension owing to the fact perhaps that his disability has been classed as being of preenlistment origin or not attributed to the war, has to depend upon the War Veterans' Allowance Act in order to get any form of compensation.
Then we have the aged veteran farmer who may be a small farmer with a family, who finds that his farm can no longer support himself, his wife and grown-up children. He turns the farm over to the son and seeks the war veterans allowances. The same thing applies to the aged veteran worker who can no longer continue at his trade and who has not been able to build up a reserve for old age,i and also applies for the war veterans allowance.
In the past we have been very fortunate in the type of men who have administered the War Veterans' Allowance Act. However, there are a number of limitations in the act which make it impossible for many of our aged veterans in need to obtain an allowance. First of all there is the ceiling on permissible income being too low. For the single veteran it is $960 and for the married veteran, $1,620. Very often we find that wives of the recipients of the war veterans allowance try to improve their condition by getting jobs and after a while they receive a notice from the war veterans allowance board to the effect that as a result of the wife's wages the joint income has exceeded the permissible income, with the result that the war veterans allowance is cut off and then later reinstated at a lower figure to make it possible for the war veterans allowance board to recover the overpayment.
On a number of occasions the Legion has asked that the allowance be raised to $1,200 for a single veteran and $2,000 for a married veteran. I have always regarded the Minister of Veterans Affairs as one of those members who have fought to achieve that objective. I was therefore somewhat surprised yesterday when he interjected while

the hon. member for Kootenay West was speaking. I quote from Hansard at page 802:
It was a great disappointment to the veterans all across Canada that the government did not see fit at that time to raise the ceiling. I did mention that the Canadian Legion had recommended a certain ceiling but I did not say that was the ceiling I was recommending. I said "raise the ceiling".
It may be true that in the instance the minister was referring to he was not advocating that the ceiling be $1,200 for single veterans and $2,000 for married veterans.
But the minister must recall that on a number of occasions in the house or in the veterans affairs committee he has advocated not only that the ceilings on permissive income be raised to $1,200 for single veterans and $2,000 for married veterans but that he actually voted in favour of those ceilings. For fear the Minister of Veterans Affairs has forgotten just what he has done in the past let me refer him to the report of the committee on veterans affairs dated Thursday, March 24, 1955, page 139. A motion was moved by Mr. White of Hastings-Frontenac, seconded by Mr. Green, as follows:
That the committee recommend that the government give consideration to introducing legislation during the present session of parliament which will have the effect of providing for amendments to this bill that will substitute $1,200 for $840 in section 1, column 3 of schedule A, and $120 for $108 in sections 2 and 3 of column 2 in schedule A, and $2,000 for $1,440 in sections 2 and 3, column 3 of schedule A.
It is interesting to note that when the vote was taken those who suported that amendment were Messrs. Brooks, Dinsdale, Gillis, Hahn, Harkness, Herridge, Pearkes, Quelch and White. I notice that the name "Green" is not there. I presume the Minister of Public Works was not present in the committee that day because I am sure if he had been not only would he have voted for the amendment but he would have filled two or three extra pages of the report of the proceedings speaking in support of it.
Therefore, while the minister may be right that at the time referred to by the hon. member for Kootenay West he was not supporting the idea of permissive income ceilings being raised to $1,200 and $2,000, nevertheless he is on record as having fought and fought persistently to achieve that objective in the past and, as I say, has not merely supported it vocally but has voted in favour of it.
It is interesting to note that in the United States the ceiling under the comparable legislation is even higher than that advocated by the Legion. In the United States the legislation comparable with the war veterans allowance is known as the disability pension,
War Veterans' Allowance Act and I quote from a world war I fact sheet put out by the veterans administration of the United States. They make this comment:
Disability compensation and disability pension should not be confused. Compensation is payable to eligible veterans, whose disabilities are due to service. Pension is payable to veterans whose total and permanent disabilities are not due to service.
At the age of 65 these pensions can be paid even though the veteran is not disabled. With regard to the ceilings on their income, I quote again:
The pension is payable only if the veteran's income does not exceed $1,400 a year without dependents, or $2,700 if he is married or has a minor child.
In addition to these amounts the veteran is allowed his social security which in some cases would amount to several thousands of dollars. In so far as permissive income is concerned, the United States legislation is far more generous than ours. It is true that in some respects the legislation is not as good -for instance, the amount of the allowance. I quote again from the report.
The monthly rate is $66.15 which is increased to $78.75 after ten years or when the veteran reaches age 65.
You will note that a single veteran is very much better off than a single veteran in this country but they do not differentiate between single and married veterans. On the other hand, if the veteran is totally disabled the amount of the pension can be increased to $135.45 a month. So I think it is only fair to say that the United States legislation comparable with the war veterans allowance is very much more generous.
Our legislation is not too bad for the veteran who is able to work because he can take advantage of section 4 or he may obtain casual earnings of $50 a month or $600 a year. Unfortunately, however, the disabled veteran who is not able to work is not in that position. The present Minister of Veterans Affairs has argued the case of the disabled veteran eloquently in the house and committee on a number of occasions. Let me refer to what the minister said, as found on page 1734 of Hansard of March 4, 1955. At that time the minister stated:
The employable veteran can take advantage of casual earnings, and I commend the minister and the department upon their definition of casual earnings and extending casual earnings so that a man will be able to earn an average of $50 a month. Also the single employable veteran can take advantage of section 4 of the act. The same applies to the married veteran who is employable: he can take advantage of section 4 and also of the casual earnings.
The veteran who loses out is the man with a small pension. His pension and his war veterans allowance now have a ceiling beyond which he cannot go, and he may not be employable.
822	HOUSE OF
War Veterans' Allowance Act
I would say that at the present time we discriminate quite severely against the recipient of war veterans allowance who is disabled and unable to work compared with the veteran who is able to work. Surely the main purpose of the act should be to take care adequately of the man who has been disabled as the result of his war service and is not able to supplement his allowance by earnings.
I want to refer to a table to show the effect that this legislation has upon these two classes. For instance, take a single veteran who is able to work. He can have casual earnings of $50 a month, making a total of $600 a year. He can have war veterans allowance of $60 a month, making a total of $720 a year. He is allowed other income of $20 a month, making a total of $240, which means that the single veteran who is able to do odd jobs can earn and receive as much as $1,560.
Compare the case of the single veteran who is able to work with that of a single veteran who is disabled and unable to work and receives a small disability pension equivalent to the amount of the casual earnings. The disability pension of $50 a month makes a total of $600. In that case the maximum amount of war veterans allowance that man is allowed to have is $30 a month instead of $60, making a total of $360 a year or an overall total of $960.
On the one hand you have a situation where the recipient of war veterans allowance who is able to do odd jobs can receive as much as $1,560 while on the other hand the recipient of war veterans allowance who suffered disabilities as the result of his war service is only able to receive a total of $960 because we do not classify his disability pension in the same way as we classify casual earnings. In other words, we classify the disability pension as income and we do not classify the casual earnings of $600 as income.
The minister has spoken strongly on that point many times and I know he feels quite sincerely about it. I gather from the way he introduced the resolution that it is not intended to deal with that matter at this time.
I am not going to criticize him on that point because I realize that he is bringing in a number of changes that are to the advantage of the veteran and it takes time to accomplish all these things, but I do hope he will give very sincere consideration to this matter so that at least at the next session of parliament the necessary changes can be made to remove what appears to be discrimination against the veteran receiving a disability pension.


The minister has referred to a number of limitations-I will call them limitations- that he intends either to remove or modify by this measure. Apparently he is going to allow the veteran to leave the country for a certain length of time without being penalized by losing his war veterans allowance. We trust that he will be able to leave for at least as long a period as a recipient of old age security can leave the country, namely six months.
Then I understand that veterans who saw service in England only, under certain conditions will be allowed to receive the war veterans allowance. I have always argued that where a veteran volunteered for service in any theatre of war he was entitled to the war veterans allowance even though he did not get beyond England because that was not his fault. He had volunteered for service anywhere. If the army found that they could use him to better advantage in England than elsewhere, the veteran should not be penalized as a consequence. I am hoping that the legislation will provide that all these veterans who volunteered for service overseas and were left in England will be eligible for the war veterans allowance.
Then the minister referred to the widows of allied ex-servicemen whose husbands died before completing 20 years residence in Canada. Those widows at the present time are not eligible. I hope the length of residence will be reduced in line with the Old Age Security Act from 20 years to 10. I think such a reduction would take care of most of the cases we have raised in the past. But even so, I feel that just as soon as the widow has completed residence in this country for the time necessary to comply with the residential requirements she should be eligible for the widows pension.
Then I am glad that the minister stated that the allowable equity in the home will be raised. He did not say by how much. The Legion have asked that it be raised from $6,000 to $9,000 which, when you consider the great increase in the cost of living and in the value of property today, does not appear to be out of line.
I again congratulate the minister on bringing down this measure. However, on the face of it, it does not appear to me to go anywhere nearly as far as is necessary to reach the objective which he himself has striven to attain time and again. I am hoping he will continue in the cabinet to fight for these things.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING ALLOWANCES, INCOME, COVERAGE, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like those who have already spoken, I welcome the amendments implied in this resolution and which will have the effect of increasing the rates

of war veterans allowance and permissible income and also of extending the provisions of the act to additional classes of veterans, veterans' widows and orphans. I am particularly happy to learn that the scope of the War Veterans' Allowance Act will be extended to include the veterans of world war I who served in the United Kingdom. I am sure this provision will be greatly appreciated by all the veterans in my province who have found the present regulations somewhat distasteful because its result has tended to give the appearance of a classification downwards in the status of their war service.
Prior to confederation all Newfoundland veterans who left the shores of Newfoundland were considered to have overseas service. They were particularly disappointed to learn that they could not be eligible for benefits under this act unless they had served in France. This arbitrary definition of a theatre of war seems to me to be somewhat illogical because since the Atlantic ocean itself was a theatre of war it was impossible for soldiers to be transported across that ocean in ships without serving in a theatre of war. This fact was vividly impressed upon me personally when the convoy in which I was being transported was chased by submarines.
Furthermore, navy veterans who served in the Atlantic retained their eligibility. It has always seemed to me to be a bit absurd to maintain that a naval man while crossing the Atlantic served in a theatre of war but that a soldier who crossed the Atlantic did not. This regulation which limited the theatre of war to continental Europe is also extremely unfair and unjust for the simple reason that no soldier has any control over his movements. He has no choice as to his sphere of service; he must obey orders. He must go where he is told to go and must stay where he is put. As the hon. member for Acadia has just pointed out, many veterans were kept in Britain by the order of their superior officers because, in their judgment, that was where their particular services were most needed. It seems to be extremely unfair to penalize a veteran for obeying orders which are designed to enable him to serve his country with maximum efficiency and effectiveness.
This arbitrary definition which says that the east side of the English channel, is a theatre of war but the west side is not has resulted in some paradoxical rulings. For example, a veteran who crossed the English channel to play on a football team would acquire eligibility merely by crossing the channel and landing on the coast of France while his comrades in Britain who were not so fortunate would not do so. Also it was
War Veterans' Allowance Act possible for a veteran to cross the channel, land on the coast of France, go out and get drunk, break his leg, get shipped back to England the next day but he would have acquired eligibility for war veterans allowances. It should be remembered that in the last phase of the war the front line was some distance from the coast of France and that the only difference between the veteran who crossed the channel and the one who stayed in England was that the former was about 20 miles nearer to the front line.
I note that the minister's statement yesterday indicated that a minimum period of service in the United Kingdom will still be required before world war I veterans can attain eligibility. For the reasons that I have just outlined, I urge him to remove this restriction completely and to extend eligibility to all veterans who left the shores of Canada. The ranks of world war I veterans are thinning fast. Every year more and more answer the final roll call. The number is rapidly diminishing. Consequently the recurring charge on the federal treasury for this group of veterans is one that will get smaller year by year.
I also urge the minister to extend eligibility to members of the merchant navy and to members of the rescue tug service. The role of the merchant navy I think was notably dramatized by the glorious exploits of the Jervis Bay. In my own particular riding the casualties in the merchant navy outnumbered those in other services and in some cases were greater than those in all other services combined. In one little community in my riding, with less than 1,000 population, 14 men made the supreme sacrifice in the merchant marine. Many of those men in the merchant navy were torpedoed more than once and spent hours and hours floating around in the water and drifting around the ocean in very small boats.
I know that the argument has been used in the past that the merchant navy received extra pay which was somewhat greater than the scale of pay granted to the armed services. In this respect I would like to point out that the members of the armed forces received war service gratuities and rehabilitation credits which the merchant navy did not get. These benefits in a very great measure compensate for the extra pay of the merchant navy; it puts them on a more equal footing and in my opinion strengthens the case of the merchant navy for their entitlement to war veterans allowances.
For the reasons which I have just mentioned and in recognition of the vital service performed by the merchant navy I urge
824	HOUSE OF COMMONS
War Veterans' Allowance Act
the minister to broaden the scope of this legislation so that its benefits may be extended to those persons who served in the merchant marine.
There are one or two other points about the veterans allowance which I would like to bring to the attention of the minister. The present War Veterans' Allowance Act regulations compel automatic suspension of war veterans allowance whenever a veteran is released from a T.B. sanatorium or from a mental institution. This works a very definite hardship because it means that in many cases the veteran is forced to return home with no adequate provision for food or fuel. I urge the minister to change this regulation so that the war veterans allowance can be continued for at least 30 days after discharge from these institutions.
This would provide sufficient time to allow the district authority to review the case and decide whether or not the allowance should be continued indefinitely.
I have a considerable number of veterans in my riding who need the benefits under the War Veteran's Allowance Act but they are not eligible because they are under 60. They do not receive a disability pension and their present ailments are ruled not attributable to war service. I think veterans all over Canada feel that awards of this nature should be based mainly on the two factors of need and service.
I do not think any veteran feels it is right that any veteran should have to depend on charity. In a good many cases veterans have come before the allowance board and their applications have not been successful because the veteran has been ruled to be not permanently unemployable. Well, in a province like mine and particularly in a riding like my own that term "permanently unemployable" is a relative one because the veteran in most cases is a fisherman. If his physical condition prevents him from fishing or working in the woods and mines then there is nothing else he can do. It is true that should he live in a city or move to a city, he might be able to get a job as a night watchman or run an elevator but there seems to be very little opportunity for assistance of this nature. Therefore I would like to see some relaxation in that particular regulation so that the district authority would have discretion to consider each case on its merits and make an award without being restricted by this requirement of having to be permanently unemployable.
In conclusion I would like to join with all those who have suggested that this legislation be referred to a committee on veterans

affairs. As the hon. member for Rosthern pointed out last night, that is the grand old tradition that has been established throughout the years in this parliament. We have always endeavoured to deal with veterans legislation on a non-party basis and I am sure the veterans throughout Canada would wish to have this tradition continued.

speechtext:
I was disappointed that the minister was not able to give us more detail last night. He mentioned that it would not be appropriate at this stage to give us full details but that indicates he has some bad news for us when he presents the bill. His colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare did give us a great deal of detail in connection with the resolutions of which we have disposed.
Like all the others who have spoken I am very glad this resolution is before the house. I have the honour to represent in parliament a great many veterans of world war I and world war II. Some of the names of communities in my riding will indicate this: for example, Blighty, Somme, Veterans, Souchey which were communities that existed because world war I veterans went to northern Saskatchewan where it was possible to get some free land and to receive some assistance and encouragement from the veterans department of that day.
Some hon. members who were here in the forties will recall a delegation of those old veterans who came to Ottawa to present some of their problems. They were able to point out that if they were to travel across Canada to tell the true story of their hardships they would not be a very effective recruiting committee. I think the minister is going to need the fullest co-operation of every member of this house to get from the cabinet the sort of support which he must have if we are to discharge our responsibility to the veterans of the two world wars. I mentioned that a great many of these veterans went to the frontier.
I should like hon. members to contrast the position of those veterans who are looking toward this legislation with some hope, with the treatment which this government provides for others. I find the Minister of National Defence considers he should have one dentist for every 750 men in the armed services; one dentist per 1,000 is usually considered to be a fairly reasonable proportion in the country. In fact, one dentist per 2,000 of the population can provide quite adequate service. But veterans in my riding are now living where there is not a single dentist in an area in which 45,000 people reside. A great many of these veterans on

the frontier find it difficult to get away to the city, make an appointment, receive dental treatment and pay the bill.
When one considers that the Minister of National Defence finds no trouble in getting $200 million to develop a new type of aircraft it is hard to understand why we are so niggardly with regard to the Minister of Veterans Affairs when he tries to meet his obligations. If a young man decides to join the air force in 1957 the Minister of National Defence is quite prepared to find $60,000 for the training necessary to enable him to fly a jet plane, and a nation which can spend $60,000 on training a man for military service can do something better than it has in the direction I have suggested.
The minister pays some pensions which are quite attractive. I notice the highest pension he pays amounts to $1,021 per month. Of course, one would have to be a general to qualify for that, and, unfortunately, everyone who joins the army cannot become a general. The pension paid to generals is of course not quite as generous as the highest the Minister of Justice provides in his department, $1,041 per month, but it would seem to me that the Minister of Veterans Affairs should be able to convince other members of the cabinet that a rich country such as ours can provide the wherewithal to do something more generous than it is doing now. I think one of the reasons why the previous government was defeated was its failure to recognize its responsibility for those who joined the armed services in the two world wars. Those who came back found that people did not honour the commitments which were given to them on enlistment.
Immediately after the election, the former minister of finance felt that before leaving office he should do something for the civil servants of Canada in order to enable them to meet the problem of inflation. That is a very real problem, but unfortunately many of the veterans are unable to cope with it in any way. I noted three of the civil service classifications mentioned in the newspapers at that time. Similar increases were provided all along the line in the civil service. In class 6, salaries were increased from $5,460 to $6,300, that is, an increase of $75 a month. In class 7 there was an increase from $5,700 to $6,870, an increase of $90 a month. In class 8 there was an increase from $7,000 to $8,300, or over $100 a month. The Minister of Finance authorized these increases because of a very real and disturbing Canadian problem, the problem of inflation, and I think the Minister of Veterans Affairs should be taking this fact into consideration and, if this bill is not yet in its final form, or if it is
War Veterans' Allowance Act not disposed of today, I hope he will be able to convince his colleagues that something better should be done, something, perhaps, which he had in mind but which he did not care to put down in the resolution or state last night. I think no one in this house is better informed than he is with regard to the representations made by Legion organizations across Canada. Ever since I came to parliament in 1940 the minister has been one of the most dependable members of parliament in coming to the defence of veterans.
I noticed in the February copy of The Legionary that there is a good article headed: "Write to your M.P. now". 1 presume the suggestion was that people should write before the election in order that candidates seeking office would be made aware of the fact that a great many who offered their lives in the service of their country in world war I and world war II did not enjoy the security promised to them. This article, written by Robert Macnicol, British Columbia member of the executive council, deserves careful reading. The author refers to an article which was carried in a well known Liberal publication, the Toronto Star Weekly, which says:
The answer is that not all Canadians share our national abundance. A sad contradiction in our prosperity is the fact that good times mean, not a higher, but a lower standard of living for many. Surely, in a land of plenty, in a country teeming with prosperity, our senior citizens, our recipients of mothers' allowances and others dependent on government pensions, should get more consideration. In the new year, let us resolve to find new ways of sharing our country's bounty by attending to these and similar problems. In this way we can transform "prosperity" from a national slogan to a real and meaningful way of life for all Canadians.
Then Mr. Macnicol has a very interesting section on war veterans allowances. He mentions that war veterans allowances present a complex problem, and goes on to say:
This is not a pension by right, but an allowance paid on a "means test" basis. Needless to say, and with some reason, many decent, thrifty veterans abhor this means test, although in ail fairness it ought to be stated that the vast majority of departmental investigators carry out their duties with sympathy and discretion.
I am sure there are a great many people alive in Canada who have seen service in the first world war, and it is my belief that a rich country such as ours could afford to do something better for them than it is doing at present. I have been in touch with the minister in connection with two of my veterans, Bob Morden and Bob McKeith and the minister has been giving sympathetic consideration to my correspondence. These are men whose injuries date back, in one case to 1916 and in the other to 1917. In one case it was possible to find the doctor who examined the veteran 40 years ago and that

War Veterans' Allowance Act doctor is of the opinion that the condition which is now affecting this veteran could have resulted from his war service.
Unfortunately there is nothing in the records to indicate that the condition is the result of war service.
In the other case the injury was not considered serious at the time but I am convinced that if either or both these veterans decided 40 years ago they were going to be a drag on society and never do another day's work they could have qualified for pensions. Both of them have been outstanding citizens in their respective communities. In good times and ill times they have been as successful as any people in the community and after 40 years they would not be considering appealing for consideration if it were not for the fact that extremely difficult conditions have arisen making what appeared to be a secure old age a life of uncertainty. After the lapse of 40 years between their service it is not easy for these proud Canadians to get down on their knees and beg for a little larger crust of bread.
I urge the minister to have another look at the speech he made in this house on July 6, 1956. I am sorry that time does not permit me to quote from it at length. At that time the hon. member for Royal, now the Minister of Veterans Affairs, made an excellent speech and outlined an exceptionally good case for the veterans.
The present Minister of Public Works made a moving speech reported at page 5866 of Hansard of July 11, 1956 in which he said:
Actually there is a great need today for an attack on the problems of the veteran and his dependents with renewed vigour. Yet that has not been done.
I am sure that after listening to his colleague last night the Minister of Public Works, if he were speaking freely, would again repeat that there is a great need today for an attack on the problems of the veteran and his dependents.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs did not tell us what is going to be done about permissive income but on July 11, 1956, as reported at page 5867 of Hansard, the Minister of Public Works said:
If that ceiling were raised from $840 per year to $1,200 per year for the single veteran, and from $1,440 per year to $2,000 per year for the married veteran, as requested year in and year out by the great veterans organizations of this country, then that situation to which I have referred would be met.
Perhaps the Minister of Veterans Affairs is going to tell us that these are the ceilings that will be established when the bill is brought down but I fear the fact he did not

mention it last night indicates that he has bad news for the veterans. I suggest that he read the speech delivered on July 11, 1956 by his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce as reported at page 5872 of Hansard and he should also make sure he reads the speech delivered by the Prime Minister as found at page 5897 of Hansard of July 12. At that time the Prime Minister said:
I should now like to say a word or two with reference to a matter that has been discussed on previous occasions, namely, war veterans allowances. As the situation is at the present time, the ceiling on income for single veterans is $840 and for married veterans $1,440. I find it hard to understand why the amount should not be increased to the level of that amount which, under the Income Tax Act, becomes exempt from income taxation. This question has been asked the minister before: where is the sense of fairness in this situation? Everyone is entitled to the old age pension, whether it is the Prime Minister who receives it or somebody else. Every citizen in our country is entitled to it at 70 years of age. Why should those in receipt of war veterans allowance find the amount of their old age pensions in effect reduced on the achievement of the age of 70 years? That is something that one hears universally complained about. It is something that is unjust for, by reason of the present ceilings, it places those who served and their dependents in a second class position with respect to others who did not serve. It brings about a state of affairs that is unfair and unjust and it constitutes a discrimination that cannot be justified. I ask the minister once more-as he has been asked on previous occasions-this question: Why should such a state of affairs be permitted to continue?
Now that the minister has had these words of the Prime Minister brought to his attention I am sure he will make an effort to ensure that nothing less than what was suggested by his colleagues in July of 1956 will be provided in this legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Veterans Affairs on his appointment to the post he now holds. I might say that his amiable and co-operative conduct in the past will probably make it much easier for him to obtain the support of his colleagues in this house in his effort to do a good job for the veterans of Canada. I would also like to say to him that he has been most fortunate and in these words I would like to congratulate him on the staff which he has inherited. I am sure it is the opinion of all Canadians that in his staff he has inherited a great wealth of experience and a high degree of industry and integrity.
It is perhaps fitting that the minister should bring this resolution before the house so close to Remembrance Day which falls on November 11. It cannot go unnoticed today that many of our colleagues in this house are wearing poppies in remembrance of those

who paid the supreme sacrifice and in remembrance of the many military engagements in which the veterans of Canada took part in the past.
I am sure the minister in bringing this legislation before us at this time had in mind the season of the year and the fact that our thoughts turn to those who served knowing that this might also be conducive to his encouraging his colleagues to loosen the purse strings in order to benefit our veterans.
While I welcome and support this legislation as a veteran, a Canadian citizen and a member of this house I would urge upon the minister, as previous speakers have done, that if he cannot go so far at this time as to establish a standing committee on veterans affairs he should at least refer the legislation to a special committee on veterans affairs. I know I am supported in this sugestion by the minister himself in his previous speeches inside and outside this house. We cannot forget that a committee on veterans affairs is the proper forum to which the various veterans organizations can go to present to the members of that committee their suggestions as to improvements in veterans legislation on behalf of those whom they represent.
If this legislation were referred to a committee we might be then able to determine if the minister has made adequate allowance in the legislation for the veteran who has a small pension but who might be incapacitated to such a degree that he is rendered unemployable. We could also learn if he has made provision for the veteran over 70 years of age who may find himself receiving war veterans allowance but who is associated with men in his own neighbourhood who are over 70 and who, although they may have an income of thousands of dollars per year, are still receiving the $55 per month old age pension.
I know that the minister is in favour of the establishment of a special committee on veterans affairs because when the extension of the war veterans allowance was being discussed in this house in 1955 the minister expressed himself as being most anxious to have a special committee on veterans affairs established. As a matter of fact the minister praised the veterans as reported at page 1735 of Hansard, 1955, volume II. He said:
I have confidence that when Bill No. 164 comes from the committee it will not be in the same state.
I would suggest to him that the same confidence should exist today, and possibly the bill which he has forecast by this resolution might not come back from the committee in the same state. I notice that on the resolution
War Veterans' Allowance Act the minister stated that this resolution forecasts legislation which is intended to and which will help a most deserving group of citizens. I might say that possibly if we have a special committee on veterans affairs now the minister might also find from representations made before that committee-if there is a public hearing-that he might be inclined to increase the pensions to the disabled, who are also a most deserving group of citizens. I just leave this thought with the minister and I know he will take it under very serious advisement.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have just one question to bring before the minister, but before I do so may I say I am just happy to look at him in his new position. He looks capable and he looks willing and I expect he will prove both by results. He is now in the position where he can get things done according to what he thinks is right, and if he does what he suggested ought to be done when he was on this side of the house he will be the best minister of veterans affairs who has ever sat on that side, but I doubt it. Any man who has been overseas knows what the veterans went through, knows how they risked their lives and wondered sometimes whether they would ever be spared to come out of the trenches.
For the past four years, usually twice a year, Mr. Chairman, I have advocated one thing for the veterans because I think if you want to get something done you should not have too many things on your list. You should have one thing and try to do it well. I have advocated that a veteran who spent two, three or four years in active warfare has a right to have his old age pension at 60 without a means test. On many occasions I have given examples. One especially I will give again.
A man had four Christmas dinners in the trenches in the first war. The minister will know that when he was eating his dinner in the trenches there were lots of flies and those flies were just as hungry as he was. Just imagine a person having wet feet and wet clothing eating his Christmas dinner. Any doctor will tell you that that takes years off a person's life.
Another man was asked to go out into the trenches and it was known that this trench had a considerable amount of water in it. There was no dry place in it. He was supposed to go for two days; he was there for 31 days. When he came back he had to go into hospital. You cannot tell me that that does not take years off a person's life.
Look at the number of aged veterans who have gone to their great reward. How many of them attained the age of 70? I know one
828	HOUSE OF
War Veterans' Allowance Act man in Fort William who is a little over 60 and he could not sprint with me 100 yards, much less carry out some other tests, because of what he left behind in the trenches in France. I would appeal with all the might that I have to the minister to consider this question and grant this man a pension at 60 without a means test. He might make it 65 but I like 60 far better.
I said that these veterans are growing fewer all the time. As I said, how many of them ever attain the age of 70? They have left in France something that they could not bring back with them and we are proud of them. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising for the first time in this house to speak on this resolution I am conscious of two things in particular. Firstly, that I enter on my duties here with a deep sense of humility, with the highest respect for this house and an earnest desire to do the best possible job as the representative of my constituency of Kings of the province of Prince Edward Island, and of this great country of Canada. I think, too, of my late father who at one time sat just two seats in front of this one as a privy councillor and of the high example of public service he set for me here and in the other house.
Secondly, Mr. Chairman, I am most pleased that my first effort on the floor should be in the field of veterans affairs. In my two years of hospitalization after Normandy there was plenty of time to think, to mingle with the "old sweats" of the first war, to discuss the problems of veterans, their widows and their dependents. Long before being discharged I had decided that my prime interest would be to work in the cause of the ex-servicemen, the ex-servicewomen and their dependents. Since returning to civilan life I have pursued that purpose zealously at the sacrifice of very considerable time and expense. For this I have received tremendous personal satisfaction in being able to do many things for veterans, not as much as I would have hoped sometimes, and I have been amply rewarded with their confidence by being unanimously selected for the key position in their organization in my province, to the highest one of being representative on their dominion council, which position I have held for a number of years.
May I now congratulate the Minister of Veterans Affairs on his being selected for that important office. We all know the hon.


member's exceptional interest and experience in the problems of the ex-servicemen, his splendid record of service in two wars and the high regard in which he is held in this house. In his department he is fortunate in being most capably assisted by the young member for Brandon-Souris.
It was a matter of great interest to veterans generally, Mr. Chairman, when our present Prime Minister became the first from the ranks of the veterans. It may be noted in passing that two of our leaders, the late Hon. Dr. Manion and the Hon. George Drew were in that category and had done very good work on behalf of the ex-servicemen.
When the Prime Minister first announced his cabinet the fact that no fewer than 12 of the 16 appointed were veterans was noted. There is no doubt that the affairs of the veterans will receive very earnest consideration from this government. I might add that I think this government has an unusually large quota of war veterans among its members and I feel that we shall all, regardless of party, have a very great interest in the problems of the ex-servicemen. As long as there are veterans there will always be problems to solve and I know that we shall all always give special regard to this important section of the Canadian people.
In this regard I should like to pay tribute here to the wonderful work done by the organization set up by the veterans themselves, the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League. This great society, dedicated to the welfare of veterans, has done an outstanding job in rendering assistance in framing veterans legislation and in looking after their problems generally. The work done in this regard by the officers of the Legion and their members all across Canada-and throughout the United States has been tremendous. The gratuitous effort by so many is worthy of the highest commendation of the Canadian people and I believe it is receiving the recognition it deserves.
With regard to the proposed changes in the war veterans allowance regulations, earlier this year a change was made to increase the married rate bringing it up to double that provided for a single recipient. While I feel, speaking from practical experience, that two cannot live as cheaply as one, I have had a number of complaints from single veterans that their amount should have been raised as their costs are understandably higher in proportion than those of the married veteran. I do hope that consideration will be given to the request of this class of recipients under the War Veterans' Allowance Act.

As far as permissible earnings ceilings are concerned, I believe they too should be raised. This would allow some recipients to earn a limited amount of extra money on their own and also allow more to qualify under the act. If these ceilings could be raised even somewhat from what they are it would be helpful to a goodly number of our veterans.
Another class of veterans deserving consideration are those who had service in England only in Word War I. We all know that for the purpose of war veterans allowance veterans of World War II who served in England are considered as having served in a theatre of war. To go into the history of this legislation briefly, it was established for the purpose of looking after those who were "pre-aged" due to the hardships and dangers of the trenches in Word War I. This legislation in general was broadened to include World War II veterans after that war who, in accordance with a means test, could be declared "permanently unemployable" due to health reasons, even if they had served only in England unless, of course, they were in receipt of a disability pension.
This seemed to place the World War I veteran in an unfair position and I may say in that regard that in my experience the veterans of World War II have been more sympathetic than those of world war I in discussions of the matter among veterans groups. The reason for this was that the first war veterans felt that a large number of men came to England near the end of the first conflict, some of them not of their own accord, and that they should not expect assistance as they were in the army a relatively short time and did not undergo the hardships of trench warfare which I have mentioned previously.
The recommendation that this class of veterans be looked after under the War Veterans' Allowance Act has been made by the Legion for the past number of years. Last year their recommendation included the qualification that there should have been at least one year of service in England. This should overcome the resistance by some veterans and allow a fairly large and deserving group to qualify under the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
I note that these resolutions contain many other recommendations, the details of which are not yet available. We all realize that the legislation now being proposed, as in the case of other types of legislation which has been receiving the consideration of this 23rd Parliament, is of an emergency nature and not expected to cover all the problems. At the next session it will be possible to consider the requirements in greater detail and in the committee on veterans affairs. I hope that
War Veterans' Allowance Act more and more progress will be made in solving the ever-pressing problem of the veteran and his dependents. I hope, Mr. Chairman, this resolution will receive the unanimous support of the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a relic of the first world war I must confess that when I hear hon. members speaking in the vein that the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and the hon. member for Fort William spoke this afternoon I rather feel that the man with the scythe is creeping up behind me. But, of course, they are perfectly right. We are dropping off at a very quick rate each year and will be doing so at an accelerated rate in the future.
I think that is really one of the major arguments against any opposition, if there is opposition, to increasing the permissible earnings ceilings of war veterans. In my constituency we have a great many war veterans and quite a number on the war veterans allowance. Because of climatic reasons these people go there to live and the problem is brought very forcibly to our attention. There are a number of great hardships at work due to the present rather low levels of permissible income. Many of these men are unable to hold even comparatively ill-paid jobs if they are going to hold them all year round. I have known of instances of men who had to arrange to be laid off for a certain length of time in order not to exceed the permissible income.
Another factor that I think we should consider is that the money incomes that people are getting today are in purchasing power very much lower than that same number of dollars was ten or fifteen years ago. Therefore we should at least try to be as generous as we have been in the past, which we will not be unless we are prepared to take into account the depreciation of the dollar. Of course, as I say, I do not know if there is going to be any opposition to this one point, and like the hon. member for Fort William I think one should concentrate on one point. To my mind the most important of the demands of the Canadian Legion and the one that affects most veterans is the raising of the level of permissible income.
I had hoped that there would be no question, since the events of last June, that when the act was amended it would be amended in line with the demands of the Canadian Legion. Last night I was a bit disturbed, in the same way that the hon. member for Acadia was, by the interjection of the minister which suggested that he and his colleagues were not accepting the levels suggested by the Canadian Legion as the proper

War Veterans' Allowance Act levels. II that is so, I would hope that the members of the present government would perhaps do what my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West, apparently has been doing and consult the records of Hansard for previous years. For instance, I hope that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce will consult Hansard of March 7, 1955 in which he will find these words included in a very moving speech he made on that occasion with regard to the position of veterans. He makes reference to the then minister's remarks and says, as found at page 1769 of Hansard:
The minister's remarks the other day I thought were cold, unsympathetic, confusing and unconvincing. He attempted to equate the ceilings of war veterans allowance with the rates for disability pensions. What purpose this procedure served I am at a loss to know. I can well remember when world war II began to develop hearing ministers representing the Liberal party say on the floor of the house, "We shall so manage the affairs of this war that no one shall be any worse off because he went overseas and no one shall be any better off because he remained at home". In the light of the almost ghastly picture which has been painted, even here this afternoon, that statement was almost full of sound and fury, signifying nothing. Although many things were done by the Liberal administration for the soldiers of world war II, nevertheless many things were left undone.
I remember, and will always do so, one experience I had with a friend in my constituency whose home I occasionally visit. This man loved to keep chickens. He was a chicken fancier. He was able to produce eggs successfully. He was a successful gardener. I went to his home one time and he said to me, "You know, Mr. Blackmore, I have got to sell all my chickens and plow up my garden because they have been around to see me and they are going to cut off my

pension because of my chickens and my garden". He was a man who had risked his life and lost his health in the struggle for his country. Yet his country was so mean and niggardly that it could not even let him raise chickens and have a garden without penalizing him by a deduction or a threatened deduction from his war veteran allowance. Probably no more needs to be said.
I am told by the hon. member for Acadia of one experience he had while he was overseas. Hon. members no doubt know that the hon. member for Acadia had a distinguished career in the army as he has had in this parliament. He told me that one time after a hard day they were visited behind the lines by Mr. Arthur Meighen, about whom we all know. Mr. Meighen warmed up to the occasion and said, "Now, men, when you get home your country will assure you that you will never lack for anything". Nothing more needs to be said.
Mr. Chairman, I hope that before very long we shall have removed many of the painful and rankling inequities or injustices which now fill our whole scheme of things in taking care of our veterans.

Mr. Chairman, I have the honour to represent here the beautiful constituency of Gaspe which, considering its population, is among those that gave the greatest number of soldiers to the country. Gaspesians are not slow to answer the call of duty. Those brave people were not afraid to leave their homes, relatives and even their children to defend our country, our democracy.
Many of those valiant men died on the battlefields and we shall have a thought for them next Monday.
Many of those veterans came back, and they had every reason to expect special consideration on the part of the government. However, Mr. Chairman, such consideration was not always commensurate to the courage they displayed on the battlefields. I wish to congratulate and thank the hon. Minister of


Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks), as well as the government for the special consideration they are now giving these veterans in the course of this first session.
However, in my constituency there is a rather peculiar situation, one which indeed appears really strange to me. A large number of ex-servicemen who were classed A-l on enlistment have returned in no condition to do any further military service. However, when they apply for a pension they are told simply that the disability they have is a pre-enlistment condition. That seems to me to be an extraordinary situation. If these people were classed A-l, it would seem that after enlistment they should draw a pension worthy of the gallantry with which they served on the battlefield.
I have seen even more than that in my constituency. I must say that I have always paid particular attention to Gaspe ex-servicemen. There is one case which I would like to refer to especially. The man in question is aged 64, served during the last war and was captured in Hong Kong. As he is now ailing, he asked to be treated at the Veterans' Hospital in Quebec. He had to travel a distance of 500 miles and then pay for the treatment which he thought he was entitled to receive free of charge. Had he thought for one moment that he would have to pay for his hospital care, I am sure he would have gone to a Gaspe hospital.
What happened? At the time he was receiving a monthly pension of $22.90. His hospitalization bill amounted to $182, and each month the authorities deduct $20 from his pension and send him the balance of $2.90.
Well, Mr. Chairman, this is a situation which the government should correct. So I say that if the government wants to give special consideration to Gaspe veterans, it must first of all appoint officials who will look after them. It should also appoint a pensions advocate for the veterans of the Gaspe constituency, so that they will not have to travel 500 miles to interview the department's advocate at headquarters.
Mr. Chairman, I wanted to bring this situation to the attention of the house and I am confident that, with the good intentions of the government and the beneficial legislation it now proposes, it should find it possible to open an office in the Gaspe constituency where an advocate will be responsible for looking after the veterans of that area.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to make a statement on second reading but there are a few remarks I should like to make at the present time. I have taken note of the many points which have been raised by hon. members, and there will be full opportunity given, of course, to debate and to discuss these points later on on second reading.
I would like to take this opportunity, though, of thanking the hon. member for Rosthern, the hon. member for Kootenay West, the hon. member for Acadia and many others who have spoken for the very kind remarks they have made concerning myself. I do not think they are altogether deserved, but I must say that in the many years I have been in this house and discussed veterans affairs in committee and in the chamber it has been a great pleasure for me to have been associated with the hon. members I have mentioned and the others who have spoken. We are all interested in one thing, that is, the benefit of the veterans, and I think it is our intention to do the very best we can for them under the rules and regulations, and under the circumstances as we find them.
The one matter I wish to discuss today has to do with the setting up of a veterans committee. I have been interested in listening to the remarks made by different members on past history. One of the greatest sports in this house over the years has, I find, been the discussion of what hon. members said years ago. I may say I am not in the least embarrassed by anything I have said in the past regarding veterans affairs or regarding the setting up of a committee. I have always been in favour of a permanent committee on 96698-53
War Veterans' Allowance Act veterans affairs being set up in the House of Commons and I am still of the same opinion.
However, Mr. Chairman, I may say that I feel that this is rather a special session, if I may call it such. This session, as has been pointed out by various hon. members at different times, has been more or less a session devoted to dealing with unfinished business, the unfinished business of the last session when the estimates of the house were not dealt with except, I believe, the post office estimates. As a matter of fact these two bills which I am introducing, and other bills which were introduced, indicate that the business of the house was not finished at the last session of parliament. The War Veterans' Allowance Act would have had to be amended this session under any circumstances. Hon. members opposite will recall that a bill was passed called an omnibus bill which provided for increases in old age security, provided for certain changes in the War Veterans' Allowance Act and also for certain changes in the Pension Act. As I said a moment ago, this unfinished business has to be dealt with by us this session.
The two acts which the Department of Veterans Affairs is bringing before the house are not controversial. The subject matter of these bills have been discussed in this house and in the veterans affairs committee on many occasions. There is the question under the War Veterans' Allowance Act of making Great Britain a theatre of war; there is the matter of the imperial veterans; there is the matter of deleting section 8 of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. All these matters have been discussed time and time again in this house and in committee. As far as the proposed pension amendments are concerned, the same applies, as hon. members will see. I would ask them to wait until they get the bill, and I am sure they will agree with me that there is no great reason why the veterans affairs committee should be set up during this session.
I may say, and both the hon. member for Kootenay West and the hon. member for Selkirk have pointed this out, that we are faced with an unusual situation, and it is our feeling that it is most desirable in present conditions to ensure that the additional benefits given to veterans by this bill are made available to them without delay. The social security acts have been passed providing for pensions and allowances for older citizens. It is, I think, quite right that without delay the same benefits should be provided for our war veterans. We all know that to set up a committee takes time; we all know that it is necessary to bring in different organizations from different parts of the country, and this, to my mind, would only delay the passing of this measure and only delay the opportunity

War Veterans' Allowance Act tor veterans to receive the benefits which we wish them to have as early as the recipients of benefits under the other acts I have mentioned.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, there is nothing controversial in these two bills. I have spoken to the head of the Canadian Legion and without divulging to the Legion what is in our bills I learned that the Legion is of the opinion that it would be more satisfactory if a permanent committee on veterans affairs were to be set up at the beginning of the next session at which time veterans legislation which might be submitted to it including the Veterans' Land Act, the War Veterans' Allowance Act, the Pension Act and others could be reviewed. The Legion indicated it would much prefer to have a permanent committee established at the beginning of next session and I believe the various veterans organizations across this country are of the same opinion. If this were done there would be no loss of time and, as I said a moment ago, we would not withhold from the veterans for some time the benefits accruing to them under the proposed amendments.
I wish to make it clear that I have not changed my opinion as far as the setting up of a permanent committee on veterans affairs is concerned. I am of the same opinion today as I was when I sat on the other side of the house. However, I do not think any good purpose would be served by setting up a committee at this time and, as a matter of fact, I think it would be to the detriment of the veteran.
I am satisfied that when hon. members opposite see the bills which are to be presented containing the amendments to the War Veterans' Allowance Act and the Pension Act they will agree with me in this respect. I hope every effort will be made by all hon. members of the house to expedite this legislation as quickly as possible.
I do not say this in a critical manner but it does seem rather strange to me that some of my hon. friends on the government side of the house should say that we should set up a committee to study this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has referred to the position taken by the present members of the opposition when they formed the government in regard to matters such as this being referred to a committee and because he has done so I think I should say a word in regard to that.
The attitude taken by the Liberal government last spring was that while there was not time to amend the veterans legislation it was desirable to make some improvement in the position of war veterans and the increases were introduced as part of the estimates. The attitude taken at that time by the official opposition and particularly by the present Prime Minister, who was then in opposition, was a very strong one. He emphasized what he claimed was upholding the rights of parliament. During the subsequent campaign he said he was going to adhere to the stand he had taken without deviation from it and without flinching. One of the reasons for the position he took in attacking the government for not referring these matters to a committee was that by refusing to do this the government was flouting the rights of parliament. The reason I am speaking at this stage, Mr. Chairman, is to ask the Minister of Veterans Affairs to consider what his oym leader said in regard to this very matter.
What the present government has to answer for is not what the Liberal government did which was so severely criticized by the present government when in opposition and particularly by the Prime Minister. They went to the people on this ground more than any other and won support and I think they are now honour bound to pay some attention to the basis on which they achieved their support. They should not turn around and say, "We are not going to do it because you

did not do it." Surely to goodness this is not going to be the attitude adopted by the present government toward the promises it made and upon which they presumably got a great deal of support.
Before the minister absolutely closes the door on this question, as already stated, I would like to draw to his attention for consideration what his leader said on April 11 of this year in regard to this very subject. I would ask the minister to bear in mind that his party requested an election as early as possible and if we were to make improvements in veterans legislation such matters had to be disposed of as early as possible- practically at once-or else we could not have had an election on June 10. In spite of the attitude of the opposition of that day that these things should be done for the veteran and an election held without delay, what did the present Prime Minister say at that time? There is no adequate opportunity for discussion here. These pension increases deserve an opportunity for full discussion. speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. Brooks (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Pension Act to place dependants of persons who served in world war II in a position comparable to that of dependants of persons who served in world war I in cases of disability or death due to improper conduct: to ensure that pensions may be paid to the dependants of deceased members of the forces resident and domiciled in Newfoundland; to provide for the continuation of disability pensions and widows' pensions to the end of the month in which death occurred except in cases where no additional pension for dependants is payable; to provide for the payment of pension to the daughter of a pensioned widower where the domestic establishment is maintained after his death; to provide for an increase in the clothing allowance on account of amputation or use of appliances; to provide for an increase in the allowances for funeral and burial expenses; to remove the limitation on the amount of pension payable to a dependent parent of a deceased pensioner after discontinuance of pension to other dependants; to authorize payment of widows' pensions at current rates upon reinstatement of discontinued pensions; and to remove the limitation on payment of pensions to or in respect of children born after a specified date, or to wives whose marriage to a member of the forces or a pensioner took place after a specified date; such measure to include, in addition, certain consequential and clarifying amendments.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Courtemanche in the chair.
